reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Refers specifically to hypercortisolism caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, the commonest cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome
Clinical features include central obesity, a rounded plethoric face, dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads, wide purple striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, and skin thinning
Metabolic consequences include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, osteoporosis, and susceptibility to infection
Diagnosis proceeds in two steps: first confirming cortisol excess, then determining whether it is ACTH-dependent and localising the source
Confirmatory tests of hypercortisolism include late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, and failure of cortisol to suppress with low-dose dexamethasone
In ACTH-dependent disease, distinguishing a pituitary source from ectopic ACTH secretion may require high-dose suppression testing, CRH stimulation, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling
Because corticotroph adenomas are often small, pituitary MRI can be normal, so biochemical and sampling data guide localisation
First-line treatment is selective transsphenoidal removal of the adenoma, with radiotherapy, medical therapy, or bilateral adrenalectomy reserved for persistent or recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Cushing disease is driven by a benign corticotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that autonomously secretes ACTH, partially escaping normal cortisol negative feedback. Persistent ACTH stimulation causes bilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia and chronic overproduction of cortisol. Sustained glucocorticoid excess produces the catabolic and metabolic features of Cushing syndrome, including protein breakdown, central fat redistribution, insulin resistance, immune suppression, hypertension, and bone loss. Retained but reset feedback sensitivity underlies the utility of high-dose dexamethasone suppression in distinguishing pituitary from ectopic sources.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-Cushing states (severe obesity, alcohol excess, depression)
Metabolic syndrome and poorly controlled diabetes with cushingoid features
Polycystic ovary syndrome for overlapping features
additionalInvestigations: Late-night salivary cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol
Plasma ACTH to establish ACTH dependence
High-dose dexamethasone suppression and CRH stimulation testing
Pituitary MRI and, when needed, inferior petrosal sinus sampling
Assessment for complications: glucose, blood pressure, bone density, electrolytes
redFlags: Severe hypercortisolism with marked hypokalaemia, uncontrolled hyperglycaemia, or severe hypertension needing urgent control
Opportunistic or overwhelming infection due to immunosuppression
Venous thromboembolism, to which hypercortisolaemic patients are prone
Psychosis or severe mood disturbance from cortisol excess
reference.prognosis: Successful transsphenoidal surgery achieves remission in a large proportion of patients, though recurrence can occur and requires long-term surveillance; untreated hypercortisolism carries substantial cardiovascular, metabolic, infective, and thrombotic mortality.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude exogenous glucocorticoid exposure before extensive workup
Interpreting a normal pituitary MRI as excluding a corticotroph adenoma
Confusing pseudo-Cushing states with true disease without dynamic testing
Assuming an ACTH-dependent source is pituitary without confirming against ectopic secretion
Neglecting perioperative and postoperative glucocorticoid management and thromboprophylaxis
management: Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy as first-line definitive treatment of the corticotroph adenoma
Repeat pituitary surgery or pituitary radiotherapy for persistent or recurrent disease
Medical control of cortisol with steroidogenesis inhibitors such as metyrapone, ketoconazole or osilodrostat, and pituitary-directed pasireotide or cabergoline
Bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory disease, with lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement and monitoring for Nelson syndrome
Perioperative and postoperative glucocorticoid cover and treatment of the resulting secondary adrenal insufficiency
Manage complications including hypertension, diabetes and osteoporosis, with venous thromboprophylaxis for the raised thrombotic risk
Long-term biochemical surveillance for recurrence through a pituitary multidisciplinary team
